items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: Archaeologists excavating a Han dynasty tomb at Mawangdui, China, in 1973 recovered a silk manuscript decorated with rows of meticulous ink ______ in the second century BCE and labeled with predictions of war, famine, or other calamities, these depictions of comets constitute one of the earliest surviving comet atlases.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a silk manuscript decorated with rows of meticulous ink figures.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Painted in the second century BCE and labeled with predictions of war, famine, or other calamities,” which describes its subject, “these depictions of comets,” and then gives the main verb “constitute.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “painted in the second century BCE ...” describe the figures in the first sentence, so the main clause “these depictions of comets constitute ...” is then joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “figures painted in the second century BCE ...” keeps the phrase inside the first sentence, and the main clause “these depictions of comets constitute ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “That were painted ...” makes the phrase a description of the figures inside the first sentence, so the main clause “these depictions of comets constitute ...” is still joined to it with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and science (Mawangdui silk comet chart, Han dynasty tomb of about 168 BCE). Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): opener of 16 words, a past participle attachable to clause 1's last noun; cue outside a 6-word window; run 50 words; reasoning steps 3. Option menu of a872c60a (tenets. Developed / tenets developed / tenets that, developed / tenets, developed). No logic-wrong distractor (the template's band-7 models have none).
band7_moves: opener of 16 words, a past participle with its own series commas that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (figures painted ...)
comma, glued and that-were options hold until the splice at “these depictions of comets constitute,” 17 words after the blank
one-sentence run of 50 words

band7.why: S1_period with a 16-word past-participle opener that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (figures painted ...), a872c60a menu; the splice shows only at “these depictions of comets constitute,” 17 words after the blank; run 50.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long noun-phrase opener
items.passage: In the 1950s, Belgian-born anthropologist Daniel Biebuyck documented several performances of a Nyanga oral epic known as ______ narrative about a hero who emerges from his mother’s middle finger already able to speak and who survives his father’s attempts to destroy him, the epic intersperses narration with songs and proverbs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “a Nyanga oral epic known as Mwindo.” The second sentence opens with the noun phrase “A narrative about a hero who emerges from his mother’s middle finger already able to speak and who survives his father’s attempts to destroy him,” which describes its subject, “the epic,” and then gives the main verb “intersperses.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: “Which is a narrative ...” keeps the description inside the first sentence as a comment on Mwindo, so the main clause “the epic intersperses narration with songs and proverbs” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “Mwindo a narrative about a hero” runs two noun phrases together, and the main clause “the epic intersperses ...” then follows the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The comma makes “a narrative about a hero ...” an appositive describing Mwindo in the first sentence, so the main clause “the epic intersperses ...” is joined to the first main clause with only the comma after “him,” a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Mwindo epic of the Nyanga, eastern DR Congo; Biebuyck recorded it in the 1950s, published 1969). Band-7 checks: opener of 23 words, an appositive noun phrase attachable to the epic's name (0fa289a7 point 3); cue outside a 6-word window; run 50 words; reasoning steps 3. Menu of 0fa289a7. Different opener type from w5b1_01 (noun phrase vs past participle).
band7_moves: opener of 23 words, a noun-phrase appositive that reads as a description of clause 1's last noun (Mwindo, a narrative about ...)
comma and which-is options hold until the splice at “the epic intersperses,” 24 words after the blank
one-sentence run of 50 words

band7.why: 0fa289a7 shape and menu: a 23-word noun-phrase appositive that reads as a description of “Mwindo” until “the epic intersperses” arrives 24 words later; every wrong option is a natural reading for most of the run.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a prepositional opener
items.passage: Frost quakes are minor seismic disturbances that typically occur on still, frigid nights following heavy rainfall or melting ______ a few hours of an abrupt temperature drop, water saturating the ground freezes and expands, generating pressure until the frozen soil and bedrock fracture with a loud boom that can rattle nearby windows.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “following heavy rainfall or melting snow.” The second sentence opens with the introductory phrase “Within a few hours of an abrupt temperature drop,” followed by its subject, “water saturating the ground,” and its verbs, “freezes and expands.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “water saturating the ground freezes and expands ...” to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice; the time phrase “within a few hours of an abrupt temperature drop” does not change that.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “melting snow within a few hours of an abrupt temperature drop” attaches the time phrase to the first sentence, and the main clause “water saturating the ground freezes ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “Which within a few hours ...” begins a relative clause that never gets its own verb before “water saturating the ground freezes,” so the sentence is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (frost quakes, or cryoseisms). Band-6 shape (2.10, 886dc9f9): a prepositional opener of 8 words; the glued reading (melting snow within a few hours ...) is natural, and the splice appears at “water saturating the ground freezes,” 9 words after the blank. One-sentence run of 53 words. No band-7 move intended.

band7.why: Planned band 6: an 8-word prepositional opener (the band-6 opener type, 886dc9f9), splice 9 words after the blank; a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (contrast with the previous sentence), semicolon after it
items.passage: Under South Korea’s jeonse system, tenants pay no monthly rent but instead give landlords a substantial deposit, often exceeding half the property’s value, and the full amount is refunded when the lease expires. The arrangement is far from free for ______ they sacrifice the interest that such a considerable sum could otherwise have earned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first clause of the second sentence, “The arrangement is far from free for renters,” corrects what the previous sentence suggests (paying no rent and getting the whole deposit back sounds free), so “though” belongs to that clause and is set off from it by a comma. The semicolon after “though” then joins the second main clause, “they sacrifice the interest that such a considerable sum could otherwise have earned,” which explains what the cost is.

A.why_wrong: With no semicolon, “though” becomes a subordinating conjunction heading “though they sacrifice the interest ...,” which presents the lost interest as a contrast to the arrangement having a cost; in fact the lost interest is that cost.

C.recipe: logic-wrong adverb placement (semicolon before a dependent clause)
C.why_wrong: The semicolon puts “though” at the head of the second part, making “though they sacrifice the interest ...” a dependent clause, which cannot follow a semicolon, and it wrongly sets the lost interest against the claim it supports.

D.why_wrong: The comma after “though” joins the two main clauses, “The arrangement is far from free for renters, though” and “they sacrifice the interest ...,” with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: social science (South Korea's jeonse lump-sum deposit leases). Band-7 checks: menu of 5aa171de (pristine, though / pristine, though; / pristine; though / pristine, though,); the contrast is with the previous sentence (no rent, deposit refunded in full), so the semicolon after “though” is the only reading in which clause 2 supports clause 1; logic-wrong distractors 2; cue in another sentence; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, whose claim (far from free) corrects the impression left by the previous sentence
two logic-wrong distractors (, though / ; though) that fail only against the previous sentence
clause 2 elaborates clause 1 rather than contrasting with it

band7.why: 5aa171de menu exactly: clause 1 (“far from free for renters”) corrects the impression of the previous sentence, so “; though” and “, though” fail only on meaning against that sentence; no option is killed by one local fact.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening clause 2 (rather), semicolon before it
items.passage: For roughly seven centuries, Vietnamese poets and scholars composed texts in chữ Nôm, a writing system derived from Chinese characters. Chữ Nôm was not merely a borrowed Chinese ______ scribes frequently combined two existing characters into a new one, with one component suggesting a Vietnamese word’s meaning and the other indicating its pronunciation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Rather” introduces the alternative to what the first clause denies: chữ Nôm was not merely borrowed, and instead scribes built new characters. So “rather” begins the second main clause, “scribes frequently combined two existing characters into a new one,” with a semicolon before it to join the two clauses and a comma after it.

B.why_wrong: The commas around “rather” leave the two main clauses, “Chữ Nôm was not merely a borrowed Chinese script” and “scribes frequently combined two existing characters into a new one,” joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark before “rather,” the two main clauses run together with no punctuation between them, a fused sentence.

D.why_wrong: The semicolon after “rather” attaches the word to the first clause, where it has no alternative to introduce; “rather” has to open the clause that gives the alternative, “scribes frequently combined two existing characters into a new one.”

items.notes: Subject: language (chữ Nôm, Vietnamese script built from and on Chinese characters, about the 13th to early 20th century). Band-6 shape of a9e5b788 (novel; rather,); L is “script”. Adverb opens clause 2 after a not-X clause; one placement distractor (rather on clause 1's side) beside a splice and a fused option.

band7.why: Planned band 6: “; rather,” after a not-X clause is the band-6 adverb shape (a9e5b788); band-7 adverb items never use rather.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (descriptor and title + name) before an infinitive
items.passage: Published in 1838, the Tagalog narrative poem Florante at Laura is set not in the Philippines but in medieval Albania. Many literary historians contend that this distant setting enabled Filipino ______ to denounce the injustices of Spanish colonial rule without attracting the scrutiny of government censors.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Francisco Balagtas” identifies which Filipino poet is meant, so it is a restrictive appositive and takes no punctuation after the title “poet.” No punctuation separates the whole noun phrase, “Filipino poet Francisco Balagtas,” from “to denounce,” the infinitive that completes “enabled.”

A.why_wrong: Setting off “Francisco Balagtas” with commas treats the name as extra information, but it is essential: it tells which Filipino poet is meant.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Balagtas” separates the noun phrase that follows “enabled” from the infinitive “to denounce” that completes it.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “poet” splits the title from the essential name that identifies the poet.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Francisco Balagtas, Florante at Laura, 1838, read as a veiled critique of Spanish rule). Band-6 title + name menu of 80aa7690 and 4dcedc31: commas around the name, single comma after title, single comma after name.

band7.why: Planned band 6: title + name before an infinitive, band-6 menu of 80aa7690 and 4dcedc31; a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (descriptor and title + name) before the main verb
items.passage: In a 1967 essay, Tanzanian ______ argued that the country’s scattered rural households should come together in cooperative villages founded on ujamaa, a Swahili word often translated as “familyhood.” In the following decade, millions of rural Tanzanians were moved into such villages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Julius Nyerere” identifies which Tanzanian statesman is meant, so it is a restrictive appositive and takes no punctuation after the descriptor “statesman.” The noun phrase “Tanzanian statesman Julius Nyerere” is the subject of the verb “argued,” and no punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma after “statesman” splits the descriptor from the essential name that identifies which statesman is meant.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Nyerere” separates the subject, “Tanzanian statesman Julius Nyerere,” from its verb, “argued.”

D.why_wrong: Setting off “Julius Nyerere” with commas treats the name as extra information, but with no article before “statesman,” the name is essential information that identifies the specific statesman meant.

items.notes: Subject: history and social science (ujamaa villagization; Nyerere's 1967 essay Socialism and Rural Development). Band-7 S4_restrictive menu of 5aae2475 and 6d4b2e1e. Local item at every band (section 6 exempts S4_restrictive from the cue-window check).
band7_moves: title + name as the subject, with the main verb right after the name (5aae2475 shape), so the comma pair and the comma before the verb both look polite
the sentence carries its own appositive comma later (ujamaa, a Swahili word ...), which invites commas at the blank
descriptor “statesman,” an occupational noun as in 5aae2475 (plant cell biologist), rather than the familiar title “president,” which cues the no-comma pattern

fixes: options, explanation and why_wrong: descriptor “president” changed to “statesman”; a familiar capitalisable title before a name cues the no-comma pattern and read band 6, now the 5aae2475 shape (occupational descriptor + name + verb)

band7.why: After the fix it is the 5aae2475 frame (intro phrase, occupational descriptor + name + verb, the band-7 menu) with a later appositive comma in the passage; before it, the familiar title “president” made the no-comma choice read band 6.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before an explanatory noun phrase with relative clauses
items.passage: Vienna’s Karl-Marx-Hof, a public housing complex that the city government completed in 1930, was closer in scale to a small town than to an apartment ______ single block that stretches for more than a kilometer and that, when it opened, housed some 5,000 residents along with laundries, baths, kindergartens, and a library.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause before the blank is complete: “Vienna’s Karl-Marx-Hof ... was closer in scale to a small town than to an apartment building.” What follows, “a single block that stretches for more than a kilometer and that ... housed some 5,000 residents ...,” is a noun phrase that explains that comparison. A colon correctly introduces such an explanation.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a single block that stretches ... and that ... housed ...” is a noun phrase: its verbs belong to the two “that” clauses, so it has no main verb of its own.

C.why_wrong: Adding “it was” turns the phrase into a main clause, which is then joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “A single block that stretches ... and that ... housed ...” as a sentence fragment: “stretches” and “housed” belong to “that” clauses, not to a main clause.

items.notes: Subject: architecture and social history (Karl-Marx-Hof, Red Vienna, about 1.1 km long, about 5,000 residents). Band-7 checks: band7 point 8 (trailing noun phrase containing finite verbs) applied to the colon template; run 53 words; the fault in A and D shows only at the end of the phrase.
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon carries two relative clauses with finite verbs (stretches, housed), so the period and semicolon options look like they start a sentence
menu of e9aee0d8 (extensive: a / ; a / , it was a / . A)
one-sentence run of 53 words

band7.why: e9aee0d8 menu; the noun phrase after the colon carries two relative clauses with finite verbs (stretches, housed), so the period and semicolon options look like they open a clause until the phrase ends with no main verb.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around a supplementary element that contains a series
items.passage: Archaeologists at Gede, near the Kenyan coast, have uncovered Chinese porcelain and Venetian glass beads acquired through Indian Ocean commerce. Gede—a Swahili settlement whose coral-stone houses, mosques, and palace were built and rebuilt over several ______ was abandoned in the early 1600s for reasons that historians continue to dispute.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “Gede” opens a supplementary element, “a Swahili settlement whose coral-stone houses, mosques, and palace were built and rebuilt over several centuries,” that comes between the subject, “Gede,” and its verb, “was abandoned.” A second dash after “centuries” closes the element, matching the first.

A.why_wrong: A comma cannot close an element that was opened with a dash; the marks around a supplementary element must match.

B.why_wrong: With no closing mark, the element opened by the dash after “Gede” never closes and runs straight into the verb “was abandoned.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot close a dash element, and it would split the subject “Gede” from its verb “was abandoned,” leaving no complete clause on either side.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Gede, or Gedi, Swahili town near Malindi, Kenya, abandoned in the early 17th century). Band-6 dash pair: partner dash 15 words before the blank; the element carries its own series commas (aacddbd8 shape: a series inside the dash element just before the closing dash), so the comma option looks natural.

band7.why: Planned band 6: partner dash 15 words before the blank with series commas inside the element (aacddbd8 shape); band-7 dash pairs nest a second level, this has one.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas, with a restrictive clause inside the first item
items.passage: A traditional sombrero vueltiao takes Colombia’s Zenú artisans weeks to make: they dry the leaves of caña flecha, a type of ______ braid the fibers into narrow strips, some blackened with mud; and stitch the strips into a spiral that forms the hat’s crown and brim.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The colon introduces a series of three actions. Because two of the items contain commas (“caña flecha, a type of cane ...” and “narrow strips, some blackened with mud”), semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon before “and stitch” shows, so a semicolon follows “rivers.” Inside the first item, “that grows along rivers” is a restrictive clause that identifies the kind of cane, so no comma comes before “that.”

B.why_wrong: The comma before “that” wrongly separates a restrictive clause from the noun “cane” that it identifies.

C.why_wrong: The semicolon after “cane” cuts the first item in two, leaving “that grows along rivers” as if it were a separate item, and the comma after “rivers” then fails to end the first item the way the semicolon before “and stitch” requires.

D.why_wrong: A comma after “rivers” cannot separate this item from the next one: the items contain commas of their own, so they are separated by semicolons, as the semicolon before “and stitch” shows.

items.notes: Subject: arts and crafts (sombrero vueltiao, Zenú weavers, caña flecha cane). Band-7 checks: two slots per option (comma before that, mark after rivers) of different rules; the series semicolon is seen only later in the sentence; run 50 words; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: blank in item 1, with the revealing semicolon (“mud; and stitch”) 10 words after the blank
second rule inside the option: a restrictive that-clause takes no comma (aaa1907f, “practice at the time;”)
series introduced by a colon, items are verb phrases with internal appositive or absolute commas

fixes: trimmed passage from 52 to 45 words (run 57 to 50, band-7 setting 38 to 50): “can take Zenú artisans in Colombia several weeks to complete” to “takes Colombia’s Zenú artisans weeks to make”, dropped “harvest and”, “together”, “continuous”; fixed contradictory run figures in notes and band7_moves

band7.why: aaa1907f shape: blank in item 1 of a semicolon series, the revealing semicolon 10 words later, and a second rule inside the option (restrictive that-clause, no comma); run trimmed to 50.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: The small flame that flickers in a rocky grotto behind a waterfall in western New York’s Chestnut Ridge ______ is fueled by natural gas seeping through fractures in the shale beneath it. A 2013 analysis found that this gas contains unusually high concentrations of ethane and propane.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first sentence is the long noun phrase “The small flame that flickers in a rocky grotto behind a waterfall in western New York’s Chestnut Ridge Park,” and its verb is “is fueled.” No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject, which ends with “Chestnut Ridge Park,” from its verb, “is fueled.”

C.why_wrong: A single dash between the subject and its verb has no role here: nothing is being set off or explained.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but the words before it are only the subject; the colon splits the subject from its verb, “is fueled.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Eternal Flame Falls, Chestnut Ridge Park, New York; a natural gas seep rich in ethane and propane). Band-6 subject-verb item (f868d438): an 18-word subject with a relative clause, prepositional phrases and a place name, so a comma before the verb feels natural.

band7.why: S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 with an 18-word subject ending in a place name.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing absolute phrase whose noun has a relative clause
items.passage: Bamana farmers in Mali once honored Chi Wara, a mythical being said to have taught humans to farm, during the planting season. Wearing carved wooden antelope headdresses fastened to basketry caps, dancers performed in the fields in male-female ______ male figure’s elongated, upright horns symbolizing the millet that farmers hoped would grow equally tall.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with “dancers performed in the fields in male-female pairs.” What follows, “the male figure’s elongated, upright horns symbolizing the millet that farmers hoped would grow equally tall,” is an absolute phrase: a noun with the participle “symbolizing” but no main verb. A comma correctly attaches it to the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the absolute phrase has no main verb: “symbolizing” is a participle, and “hoped” and “would grow” belong to the clause that describes the millet.

B.why_wrong: “And” would have to join two main clauses, but the absolute phrase after it has no main verb, so the sentence is not grammatical.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “The male figure’s elongated, upright horns symbolizing the millet ...” as a fragment, since “symbolizing” is not a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Bamana chi wara antelope headdresses, danced in male-female pairs at planting; the male's tall horns linked to the growth of millet). Band-7 checks: run 33 words; trailing absolute phrase with finite verbs inside; reasoning steps 3.
band7_moves: absolute phrase whose noun takes a relative clause with finite verbs (hoped, would grow), so the period and semicolon options look like they start a clause (band7 point 8)
menu of 62120607 (quilts, and the / quilts, the / quilts; the / quilts. The)
the fault in A, B and D shows only at “symbolizing,” 6 words after the blank, and is masked by the finite verbs later

band7.why: 62120607 menu (quilts, and the / , the / ; the / . The); the absolute phrase's noun takes a relative clause with finite verbs (hoped, would grow), so the semicolon and period options look clausal.

items.subtype: Comma plus but between two independent clauses
items.passage: When the dissolution of the Soviet Union cut off Cuba’s imports of synthetic fertilizer and petroleum in the early 1990s, residents of Havana began cultivating vegetables in raised compost beds on abandoned lots. These gardens, known as organopónicos, were conceived as a temporary ______ many of them continue to supply neighborhoods with fresh produce today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence has two main clauses: “These gardens, known as organopónicos, were conceived as a temporary measure” and “many of them continue to supply neighborhoods with fresh produce today.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together, a fused sentence.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two main clauses as long as these, a comma is needed before the conjunction.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses “These gardens ... were conceived as a temporary measure” and “many of them continue to supply neighborhoods ...”; this is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Cuban organopónicos, urban raised-bed gardens of the Special Period). Medium comma + but menu of 2.12 (skeptical but / skeptical, but / skeptical, / skeptical); the first clause has an appositive set off by commas, so a lone comma at the blank looks like part of that pattern.

items.subtype: Closing a comma pair around an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: Zeugma, an ancient city on the Euphrates River in what is now southeastern ______ was partly submerged in 2000 by the reservoir of a newly built dam. Racing against the rising water, archaeologists salvaged dozens of elaborate Roman mosaics, which the nearby city of Gaziantep now exhibits in a dedicated museum.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “Zeugma” opens a supplementary element, “an ancient city on the Euphrates River in what is now southeastern Turkey,” that comes between the subject, “Zeugma,” and its verb, “was partly submerged.” A comma after “Turkey” closes the element, matching the first comma.

A.why_wrong: With no closing comma, the appositive opened after “Zeugma” never closes and runs straight into the verb “was partly submerged.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot close an element opened by a comma, and it would split the subject “Zeugma” from its verb, leaving no complete clause before the semicolon.

D.why_wrong: A dash cannot close an element that was opened with a comma; the marks around a supplementary element must match.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Zeugma, Roman city on the Euphrates partly flooded by the Birecik Dam reservoir in 2000; mosaics now in the Zeugma Mosaic Museum, Gaziantep). Medium comma pair of 2.1: the opening comma is 12 words before the blank, between subject and verb. Replaces the ambahan draft (second Philippine poetry subject in the batch).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: In 1944, Maurie Isenberg, a radar operator stationed on remote Marchinbar Island off northern Australia, discovered nine corroded coins buried in the ______ later, researchers identified five of them as copper currency minted centuries earlier by the Kilwa Sultanate, a prosperous Swahili trading state in what is now Tanzania.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “discovered nine corroded coins buried in the sand.” The second sentence opens with the introductory phrase “Decades later,” followed by its subject, “researchers,” and its verb, “identified.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “decades later” is glued to the first sentence (“buried in the sand decades later”), and the main clause “researchers identified five of them ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “Which decades later” begins a relative clause that never gets its own verb, since “researchers identified ...” is a separate main clause; the sentence is not grammatical.

D.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “researchers identified five of them ...” to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Marchinbar Island coins found by Maurie Isenberg in 1944, five of them from the Kilwa Sultanate). Medium S1_period with a 2-word opener (Decades later), as in 2.7 and 2.9; the which-option follows 2.10 (earlier, which in).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: At the 1917 National Eisteddfod of Wales, the festival’s most prestigious poetry prize was awarded to Hedd Wyn, a young shepherd from the village of Trawsfynydd. The poet, however, had been killed in combat in Belgium several weeks ______ organizers to drape the ceremonial chair intended for him in black cloth.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause (rather)
items.passage: Cherokee playwright Lynn Riggs’s Green Grow the Lilacs, a 1931 drama set in Indian Territory, closed after a disappointingly brief Broadway engagement. items.explanation: “The play did not simply fade away” and “it lives on through Oklahoma! ...” are both main clauses, so a semicolon belongs between them. “Rather” introduces the second clause, which offers the alternative to the denied idea, so it follows the semicolon and is set off with a comma.

A.why_wrong: Commas on both sides of “rather” leave the two main clauses, “The play did not simply fade away” and “it lives on through Oklahoma! ...,” joined by commas alone, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: Nothing separates “fade away” from “rather,” so the first main clause runs straight into the second without the semicolon or period that two main clauses need.

D.why_wrong: This places “rather” at the end of the first clause, where it has no sensible meaning; “rather” must begin the second clause to introduce the alternative to fading away.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause (however), second clause explains

C.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “however,” the “because” clause can attach to the first clause, but the main clause “a blazar seen head-on looks far brighter ...” is then joined with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two main clauses run together; there is no semicolon or period between “deceptive however” and the second clause.

items.notes: Subject: science (Jedidah Isler studies blazars; relativistic beaming makes a jet aimed at Earth look brighter). Band-7 checks: logic-wrong distractor present; cue (the previous sentence’s claim) outside a 6-word window; subordinate-clause opener for clause 2 as in a05cc490; menu of 5aa171de (pristine, though / pristine, though; / pristine; though / pristine, though,) with however.

clause 2 opens with a subordinate “because” clause, so the comma-pair version hides its splice until “a blazar seen head-on,” 13 words past the blank

items.explanation: The verb “describes” has two objects joined by “and”: “how a luxurious dressing gown made his old furnishings look shabby” and “how he replaced one possession after another ....” The two parts of a compound joined by “and” are not separated by punctuation.

B.why_wrong: A comma before “and” would set off the second object of “describes,” but “how he replaced one possession after another ...” is not a main clause; it is the second part of a compound object, so no comma is needed.

C.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit; comma after the conjunction
C.why_wrong: Commas on both sides of “and” split the compound object and also separate “and” from the clause it introduces.

D.why_wrong: A comma after “and” separates the conjunction from “how he replaced ...,” the clause it joins to the first object.

items.notes: Subject: social science and philosophy (Diderot effect, named for Diderot's essay 'Regrets on Parting with My Old Dressing Gown,' usually dated 1769; the term was later coined by anthropologist Grant McCracken). Known facts. Medium shape of 2.23: a compound of two clauses joined by and after a long first element, where a comma before and feels natural; options vary only commas around and, as in 2.23.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Al Sadu is a weaving tradition practiced by Bedouin women in the Arabian Peninsula. Working on ground looms, weavers turn fibers ______ sheep, camels, and goats into tent walls, rugs, and saddlebags decorated with bold geometric patterns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “from” and its object, “sheep, camels, and goats,” form one phrase that tells where the fibers come from. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “weavers turn fibers from” is not complete; the colon splits the preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A single dash has no role here; it separates the preposition “from” from its object, “sheep, camels, and goats.”

D.why_wrong: A comma separates the preposition “from” from its object, which is not conventional.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Al Sadu, Bedouin women's weaving of sheep wool, camel hair and goat hair on ground looms for tents, rugs and camel trappings, Arabian Peninsula). Known facts, no names. Easy shape of 1.5 and 1.9: a context sentence, then the blank between a preposition and a series that is its object; four different marks.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Boulengerula taitanus is a limbless, burrowing amphibian found in the Taita Hills of southeastern Kenya. Soon after they hatch, its young feed ______ their mother’s skin, using specialized teeth to peel off its fatty, nutrient-rich outer layer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “feed on their mother’s skin,” the preposition “on” and its object, “their mother’s skin,” belong together. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A single dash has no role here; it separates the preposition “on” from its object, “their mother’s skin.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “its young feed on” is not complete without the object of “on.”

C.why_wrong: A comma separates the preposition “on” from its object, which is not conventional.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Boulengerula taitanus, a caecilian of the Taita Hills, Kenya: mothers grow a thick, lipid-rich outer skin that the young peel off and eat with specialized teeth, reported in 2006). Known biology, no names. Easy shape of 1.21 and 1.23 (embodied by, home to): verb plus preposition, blank before the preposition's object.

items.subtype: Direct question after a colon: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: Some early Greek inscriptions are written in boustrophedon, a style in which the direction of writing reverses at the end of every line, like an ox plowing a field. This style raises a question that historians still discuss: Why ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words after the colon, beginning with “Why,” ask a direct question. A direct question uses inverted word order (“did scribes choose”) and ends with a question mark.

A.recipe: question errors (period on a direct question)
A.why_wrong: The word order is correct for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

B.why_wrong: A direct question needs inverted order, with the helping verb “did” before the subject; “Why scribes chose this method?” keeps statement order.

D.why_wrong: “Why scribes chose this method.” uses statement order and a period, but the colon introduces the question itself, which must be asked directly.

items.notes: Subject: language and writing (boustrophedon, ox-turning writing in early Greek inscriptions). Known facts. Easy shape of 1.18: a context sentence, then a direct question introduced by a colon, blank ending the passage; full 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark.

items.subtype: Comma plus but between independent clauses
items.passage: Market researchers often ask consumers whether they intend to buy a product in order to forecast ______ simply answering such a question can make people more likely to buy, a pattern known as the mere-measurement effect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both sides of the blank are main clauses: “Market researchers often ask consumers whether they intend to buy a product in order to forecast sales” and “simply answering such a question can make people more likely to buy.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two long main clauses like these, a comma goes before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together after “sales.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (mere-measurement effect: asking about purchase intentions raises later purchase rates). Known finding, no names. Easy shape and menu of 1.2 (fibers, / fibers but / fibers / fibers, but): one sentence, the second clause opens with its gerund subject right after the blank, and a sentence appositive closes it.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: A tughra is an elaborate calligraphic emblem that served as the official signature of an Ottoman sultan. When a new sultan rose to the ______ court calligraphers designed a tughra combining his name with his father’s, and it appeared on decrees, coins, and even the walls of buildings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with the dependent clause “When a new sultan rose to the throne,” which must be followed by a main clause, “court calligraphers designed a tughra combining his name with his father’s.” A comma correctly separates the introductory dependent clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: The period makes “When a new sultan rose to the throne” a sentence of its own, but a clause beginning with “When” cannot stand alone, so it is a fragment.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “When a new sultan rose to the throne” is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs straight into the main clause, so “rose to the throne court calligraphers” reads as one confused string.

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (tughra, the calligraphic monogram made for each Ottoman sultan on accession, with his name and his father's, used on decrees, coins and buildings). Known facts. Easy shape of 1.6 and 1.8 (Because ..., Although ...): a context sentence, then an introductory When clause ending at the blank before the main clause's subject; menu of 1.19 (classroom. / classroom; / classroom, / classroom). Varied from item 17, whose opener is a participle.

items.subtype: Restrictive that clause: no comma, and the that is needed
items.passage: Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth dozens of times every second. In 1952, German physicist Winfried Otto Schumann predicted that these strikes would produce low-frequency radio ______ bounce back and forth between the ground and the ionosphere, a layer of charged particles high in the atmosphere.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “that bounce back and forth between the ground and the ionosphere” identifies which low-frequency radio waves Schumann predicted. A restrictive clause like this one begins with “that” and is not set off from the noun it modifies with a comma.

A.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “bounce” has no link to “waves,” so the sentence reads “these strikes would produce low-frequency radio waves, bounce back and forth ...,” which is not grammatical.

C.why_wrong: Without “that,” “radio waves bounce back and forth” is a clause dropped into the sentence with no connection to “would produce,” so the sentence is not grammatical.

D.why_wrong: A comma before “that” treats the restrictive clause as nonessential; a clause beginning with “that” is not set off with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Schumann resonances: in 1952 Winfried Otto Schumann predicted lightning-excited extremely low-frequency waves resonating in the cavity between the ground and the ionosphere; lightning strikes Earth roughly 40 to 50 times a second). Known physics. Easy shape and menu of 1.29 (company, / company that / company / company, that).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses, the second opening with its subject
items.passage: Radiolarians are single-celled organisms that drift through the world’s oceans as part of the plankton. Each one builds an intricate skeleton out of ______ skeletons often take the shape of spheres, spirals, or spiky stars, and many are barely visible to the naked eye.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Each one builds an intricate skeleton out of silica” is a main clause, and “These skeletons often take the shape of spheres, spirals, or spiky stars, and many are barely visible to the naked eye” is another. A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses “Each one builds an intricate skeleton out of silica” and “these skeletons often take the shape ....”

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together after “silica.”

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses like these, a comma goes before it; without one, the clauses are not correctly joined.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (radiolarians, single-celled marine plankton with ornate silica skeletons). Known biology, no names. Easy shape and menu of 1.14 (settings she / settings, she / settings and she / settings. She): the second clause opens with its subject right after the blank.
